Our Chimney Cleaning Process

A good cleaning is more than running a brush through the flue. Here is what you can expect when we visit your home:

  1. Preparation. We lay down protective coverings around the fireplace and set up equipment to contain soot and debris.
  2. Visual check. Before cleaning, we look at the firebox, damper, and accessible parts of the flue for obvious signs of damage or blockage.

Common Chimney Problems We Help Solve

Many chimney problems start small and grow quietly. Knowing the warning signs helps you act early.

Creosote and soot buildup

Every wood fire leaves residue behind. Creosote is a dark, tar-like or flaky deposit that can build up inside the flue. It is flammable, which is why regular cleaning matters for any wood-burning fireplace.

Chimney leaks

Water stains on the ceiling near the fireplace, damp smells, or rust inside the firebox can point to a leak. Causes include a missing cap, a cracked crown, or failing flashing.

Damaged or missing chimney caps

A cap keeps rain, animals, and debris out of the flue. When it rusts, shifts, or goes missing, problems tend to follow.

Deteriorating mortar and masonry

Crumbling mortar joints, loose bricks, and white staining on the outside of the chimney can signal moisture damage that deserves attention.

Draft and smoke issues

If smoke drifts into the room or your fire struggles to burn, the cause could be a blockage, a closed damper, or a flue problem that needs a closer look.

Chimney Cleaning and Sweeping in Fort Worth, TX

A clean chimney is one of the simplest ways to protect your home and enjoy your fireplace with confidence. Embercrest Chimney Sweep Tanglewood provides chimney cleaning for homeowners who want soot, creosote, and debris removed from the flue and firebox, along with honest feedback about the overall condition of their chimney.

Call (682) 350-5722 or request an estimate to schedule your visit.

Why Chimney Cleaning Matters

Each time you burn wood, the smoke carries byproducts up through the flue. As that smoke cools against the chimney walls, some of it condenses and sticks. The result is soot, a lighter powdery residue, and creosote, a darker deposit that can appear as a tar-like glaze or as brittle flakes. Creosote is flammable, and a heavy buildup is a recognized fire risk in wood-burning systems.

Buildup also affects how well your fireplace works. A restricted flue can cause weak draft, smoky rooms, and lingering odors. Birds, squirrels, leaves, and fallen debris can add to the problem, especially when the chimney has no cap or the cap is damaged. Regular cleaning keeps the flue clear and gives a trained eye a chance to spot trouble before it grows.

What Is Included in Our Chimney Cleaning

Every home is different, but a typical visit from Embercrest Chimney Sweep Tanglewood includes the following:

  • Protective coverings and containment equipment around the fireplace opening
  • A visual check of the firebox, damper, and accessible flue areas before cleaning
  • Brushing and vacuuming to remove soot, creosote, and loose debris from the flue and firebox
  • Notes on anything unusual, such as cracked masonry, water staining, a worn cap, or damper problems
  • A plain-language summary of what we found and what we recommend, if anything
  • Cleanup of the work area before we leave

Signs Your Chimney Needs Cleaning

You do not have to wait for an annual reminder. Call us if you notice any of the following:

  • Dark, shiny, or flaky residue inside the firebox or on the damper
  • A strong smoky or tar-like smell, especially in warm, humid weather
  • Smoke entering the room when you light a fire
  • Fires that are slow to start or do not burn well
  • Soot falling into the firebox or collecting on the hearth
  • Sounds from the flue that suggest nesting animals or debris
  • It has been a year or more since your last cleaning and you have been using the fireplace

How Often Should You Schedule a Chimney Sweep?

The right frequency depends on how often you burn and what you burn. A household that lights frequent fires through the cooler months will build up residue faster than one that uses the fireplace a few times a year. Unseasoned or damp wood tends to produce more creosote than well-seasoned hardwood, and a fire that smolders at low temperature leaves more residue than a hot, well-ventilated one.

The Chimney Safety Institute of America publishes homeowner guidance on chimney care and generally recommends that chimneys be inspected yearly, then cleaned or repaired as needed. In practice, many Fort Worth homeowners schedule their visit in late summer or early fall, before the first cold nights, so there is time to address any surprises.

Cleaning and Inspection Work Together

Cleaning removes buildup, but it does not tell you whether the chimney is structurally sound. That is why we pay attention to the condition of your chimney while we work. If we spot something that needs a closer look, we may recommend a more detailed chimney inspection so you get a complete picture of the flue, liner, and masonry.

If the issue turns out to be damage rather than buildup, such as a cracked crown, loose bricks, or a leaking joint, our chimney repair page explains the common fixes and how we approach them.

Gas, Wood, and Other Fireplaces

Wood-burning fireplaces are the most obvious candidates for regular sweeping, but they are not the only ones that benefit from attention. Gas fireplaces and inserts have their own maintenance needs, and the flue or vent that serves them can still collect debris, nests, or moisture damage. If you are unsure what kind of system you have, describe it when you call and we will help you figure out the right service.

How to Prepare for Your Appointment

A little preparation helps the visit go smoothly:

  • Make sure the fireplace has been cool for at least a day before we arrive.
  • Clear furniture, rugs, and decorations from the area around the hearth.
  • Let us know about any problems you have noticed, such as odors, smoke, or leaks.
  • Make sure we can reach the fireplace and, if needed, the roof.
  • Have any questions ready. We are happy to explain what we see.

Burning Habits That Help Keep Your Chimney Cleaner

Routine cleaning is the foundation, but your habits make a difference too. Burn dry, well-seasoned firewood, which produces less residue than green or wet wood. Avoid burning trash, cardboard, or treated lumber in your fireplace. Give fires enough air to burn hot rather than smolder, and have any change in performance checked quickly. These small steps help reduce buildup between visits, though they do not replace regular cleaning or inspection.

Common Questions About Chimney Cleaning in Fort Worth

How long does a chimney cleaning take?

Most visits take a modest amount of time, though the exact length depends on the type of fireplace, the amount of buildup, and what we find. We will give you an idea of timing when you book.

Will chimney cleaning make a mess in my home?

We use protective coverings and vacuum equipment to keep soot contained, and we clean the area when finished.

Do I still need cleaning if I rarely use my fireplace?

Possibly. Even infrequent use leaves residue, and chimneys can collect debris, nests, and moisture damage even when no fires are burning.

What does chimney cleaning cost in Fort Worth?

Pricing depends on your fireplace, the condition of the flue, and access to the roof. Contact us for an estimate.

What Is a Chimney Inspection?

A chimney inspection is a structured check of the chimney system, from the firebox up to the top of the stack. The goal is to identify damage, blockages, and conditions that could affect safety or performance. Unlike a cleaning, which focuses on removing buildup, an inspection focuses on evaluating condition and reporting what is found.

Chimney inspections are commonly described in levels, from a basic visual check of accessible areas to more detailed evaluations that may use specialized equipment to view inside the flue. The level that makes sense for you depends on your situation, such as routine annual maintenance, a recent change to your fireplace or heating appliance, a storm, or a home purchase.

What We Look at During an Inspection

While the details vary by home, a thorough inspection generally covers the following areas.

Firebox and damper

We check the firebox walls and floor for cracks or deterioration and make sure the damper opens, closes, and seals as it should. A damper that sticks or no longer fits properly can affect draft and let conditioned air escape.

Flue and liner

The liner is the interior surface that contains combustion gases and protects the surrounding structure. We look for cracks, gaps, deterioration, and signs of heavy buildup. Liner problems can be hard to spot without a proper look inside the flue.

Smoke chamber and throat

Just above the firebox, the smoke chamber guides smoke into the flue. Rough surfaces, damaged mortar, or buildup here can affect how well the system works.

Masonry and exterior

On the outside, we look at bricks, mortar joints, and the overall condition of the stack. Crumbling mortar, white staining, and leaning or loose bricks can all indicate moisture problems.

Chimney cap and crown

The cap keeps rain, animals, and debris out of the flue, and the crown is the sloped surface at the top of the chimney that sheds water. Cracks in the crown or a damaged, rusted, or missing cap can let water and pests in.

Flashing and roof connection

Flashing seals the joint where the chimney meets the roof. If it lifts or corrodes, water can find its way into the attic or walls.

When Should You Schedule a Chimney Inspection?

The Chimney Safety Institute of America and other industry sources generally advise that chimneys be inspected at least once a year. Beyond the annual check, consider scheduling an inspection in these situations:

  • You are buying or selling a home with a fireplace
  • You have had a chimney fire or suspect one occurred
  • A severe storm, hail, or high winds have affected the roof or chimney
  • You are changing a heating appliance, such as adding an insert or switching fuel types
  • You notice water stains, musty odors, or rust near the fireplace
  • Smoke is entering the room or the fire does not draw well
  • You have not used the fireplace in a long time and want to be sure it is safe

Inspection vs. Chimney Cleaning

People often ask whether they need an inspection, a cleaning, or both. Think of it this way. Chimney cleaning removes soot, creosote, and debris. An inspection assesses condition and identifies problems. They work well together, since a clean flue is easier to evaluate and an inspection can reveal whether cleaning alone is enough. If you are unsure which one you need, tell us what you have noticed and we will recommend the right starting point.

What Happens After the Inspection?

Once we have finished, we go over our findings with you in plain terms. Depending on what we found, the outcome might be one of the following:

  • No issues found. Your chimney appears to be in good working order, and routine maintenance is all you need.
  • Cleaning recommended. Buildup in the flue or firebox should be removed before the fireplace is used again.
  • Repairs recommended. We found damage such as a cracked crown, failing mortar, a worn cap, or flashing problems. We explain what each issue means and what your options are. You can read more about common fixes on our chimney repair page.
  • Further evaluation suggested. If something cannot be assessed fully with the equipment on hand, we will tell you what additional steps would help.

Inspections for Home Buyers and Sellers

A fireplace is a selling point, but it can also hide expensive surprises. If you are buying a Fort Worth home, a chimney inspection before closing helps you understand the condition of the system and plan for any repairs. A general home inspection usually includes only a quick look at the fireplace, and it may not examine the inside of the flue. Sellers can also benefit, since knowing the condition in advance lets you address problems on your own schedule instead of during a negotiation.

Warning Signs You Should Not Ignore

Some symptoms call for prompt attention rather than waiting for your next scheduled visit:

  • Water stains on the ceiling or wall near the chimney
  • Pieces of mortar, brick, or tile in the firebox or on the ground near the chimney
  • Rust on the damper, firebox, or fireplace accessories
  • A leaning, cracked, or visibly deteriorating chimney stack
  • Strong odors coming from the fireplace
  • Smoke or soot entering the room during use

If you suspect a chimney fire or smell gas, stop using the appliance and follow appropriate safety steps before calling for service.

How to Prepare for Your Inspection

Preparation is simple. Let the fireplace cool completely, clear the area around the hearth, and make a note of anything unusual you have seen or smelled. If you have records of past cleanings or repairs, keep them handy. Make sure we can reach the fireplace and have safe access to the roof or exterior where needed.

The time depends on the level of inspection, the type of chimney, and access. We will give you an estimate when you book.

Do I need an inspection if I only use my fireplace occasionally?

Often yes. Damage from weather, moisture, and animals can occur whether or not you burn fires, and a fireplace used rarely can still develop problems.

Will you inspect gas fireplaces and inserts?

The price depends on the inspection level and the chimney's accessibility. Contact us for an estimate.

Whether it is part of your annual routine, a precaution after a storm, or a step in a home sale, an inspection gives you the facts you need. What Is Tuckpointing?

Mortar joints typically deteriorate faster than kiln-fired clay brick. Tuckpointing involves carefully grinding out worn, decayed mortar to an even depth and packing fresh, color-matched mortar into the joints. This seals out moisture and reinforces the entire stack.

How Often Should You Really Clean Your Chimney in North Texas?

When living in North Texas, our winters are notoriously unpredictable. We might experience 70-degree sunshine one afternoon and a sub-freezing ice storm 24 hours later. Because our heating season is concentrated into brief, intense cold snaps, many homeowners wonder: How often does a chimney actually need cleaning if it's only used for a few months each year?

The 1/8-Inch Rule: Measuring Creosote Buildup

The standard guideline recognized by fire safety professionals is based on physical residue rather than calendar months. The Chimney Safety Institute of America recommends having your chimney swept whenever 1/8th of an inch of creosote deposits accumulate on the flue walls.

While that may sound like a very thin layer, creosote is highly combustible. During hot, roaring fires, this tar-like hydrocarbon can ignite, triggering internal flue fires that reach temperatures exceeding 2,000°F. In a masonry or prefabricated chimney, such extreme heat can crack clay flue tiles, warp metal liners, and ignite nearby attic framing timbers.

Factors Determining Cleaning Frequency for Local Homes

How quickly your chimney reaches that 1/8-inch threshold depends on several key usage patterns:

  • Frequency of Fires: Lighting a fire every weekend throughout December, January, and February generates substantially more residue than burning a decorative Duraflame log twice a year.
  • Moisture Content of Firewood: Burning green, unseasoned wood creates heavy, dense smoke that quickly cools and condenses onto cold flue tiles as sticky creosote. Well-seasoned hardwood with under 20% moisture burns cleaner and hotter.
  • Fireplace Efficiency & Burning Habits: Smoldering fires that are starved of combustion air produce significantly more unburned hydrocarbons than bright, hot, well-oxygenated fires.
  • Flue Geometry and Materials: Exterior brick chimneys exposed to North Texas wind chills cool down rapidly, causing smoke to condense much quicker than chimneys built inside interior home walls.

Why Annual Inspections Are Essential Regardless of Usage

Even if you only lit three fires all winter, annual maintenance remains vital. In the Fort Worth and Tarrant County areas, chimneys face environmental threats during the off-season months. Severe spring thunderstorms, driving hail, and intense summer heat take a serious toll on exterior chimney structures.

Furthermore, spring brings nesting birds like chimney swifts, along with squirrels, wasps, and raccoons seeking refuge inside cool flues. Scheduling a professional chimney inspection each autumn guarantees that the flue passage is unobstructed by animal nests, that the damper opens freely, and that the chimney crown has not cracked from heat stress.

Signs Your Chimney Requires Immediate Cleaning

Do not wait for a scheduled annual visit if you notice any of these warning signs:

  1. Thick, black, shiny glaze or velvety black flakes lining the firebox or throat damper.
  2. A persistent campfire or acrid barbecue smell drifting from the hearth, particularly on warm, humid days.
  3. Smoke backing up into your living room rather than drawing cleanly up the flue.
  4. Slow, sluggish fires that struggle to stay lit despite using dry kindling.
  5. Sounds of rustling or chirping originating inside the chimney column.

If you observe any of these symptoms, arranging for certified chimney cleaning before lighting another fire is the safest course of action.

Best Practices to Keep Your Chimney Clean

You can dramatically reduce soot and creosote buildup between professional cleanings by adopting a few simple burning habits:

  • Only burn seasoned hardwoods like Texas post oak, pecan, or hickory that have dried for at least six to nine months.
  • Never burn treated construction lumber, painted wood, cardboard, or wrapping paper, all of which release toxic fumes and volatile chemicals.
  • Warm the flue before lighting a full fire by holding a rolled newspaper torch near the damper to establish an upward draft.
  • Keep the glass doors or mesh spark curtains closed while burning to prevent stray sparks from escaping.

blogs.contentHtml:
The 3 Stages of Creosote: Identification, Risks, and Removal

Every time you burn wood in your fireplace, the combustion process produces smoke, water vapor, unburned wood particles, and condensed hydrocarbon gases. As these gases travel up the chimney flue and encounter cooler air, they condense along the liner walls into a dark, combustible byproduct known as creosote. However, not all creosote looks or behaves the same way.

Understanding Creosote Progression

Creosote develops across three distinct stages, with each subsequent stage becoming denser, harder to remove, and significantly more hazardous. Understanding these stages empowers homeowners to address buildup before it creates catastrophic chimney fire conditions.

Stage 1: Flaky, Sooty Creosote

Stage 1 creosote appears as loose, dry, powdery soot or velvet-like black dust. It forms when there is relatively complete combustion, good air circulation, and a warm flue. Because Stage 1 deposits contain high air volume and low moisture density, they are the easiest type of creosote to remove.

A chimney professional using standard wire or stiff polypropylene brushes during routine chimney cleaning can easily sweep Stage 1 soot away from clay or stainless steel chimney walls, leaving the liner clean and safe for continued burning.

Stage 2: Crunchy, Tar-Flake Creosote

Stage 2 creosote occurs when air supply is restricted or when the chimney flue remains consistently cool. This commonly happens in fireplaces with glass doors kept tightly closed without sufficient air intake, or when burning wood with excessive moisture content.

Stage 2 deposits look like dark, shiny, hardened flakes or black popcorn-like crusted chips. Chemical analysis reveals concentrated tar and pitch content. While a standard sweep brush cannot easily dislodge Stage 2 creosote, specialized rotary power sweeping equipment with spinning chains or heavy whips can shatter and scrape away these brittle deposits safely.

Stage 3: Glazed Creosote (The Critical Fire Danger)

Stage 3 creosote, commonly referred to as glazed creosote, is the most dangerous condition a chimney can develop. It resembles a thick, slick, pitch-black layer of hardened lacquer or dried roadway tar poured across the flue interior.

Glazed creosote forms under extreme conditions: severely restricted draft airflow, oversized chimney flues, or the repeated burning of green, unseasoned firewood. Each time fires are lit, lighter volatile compounds burn off while heavier tars boil and re-harden, creating an impenetrable fuel crust. Stage 3 creosote has an extremely low ignition temperature. Once lit, it behaves like concentrated rocket fuel inside your chimney, burning at temperatures exceeding 2,100°F.

Why Stage 3 Creosote Cannot Be Brushed Away

Traditional manual brushing tools cannot budge Stage 3 glazed creosote. Striking it with excessive mechanical force risks cracking clay flue liners or puncturing metal pipes. Eliminating Stage 3 glaze requires advanced professional intervention:

  • Chemical Treatments: Technicians apply specialized chemical modifier sprays or powders over several weeks. When heated by subsequent controlled fires, these chemicals break the chemical bonds within the tar, transforming the glaze into a brittle, sweepable Stage 2 crust.
  • Rotary De-glazing Equipment: In severe cases, technicians deploy specialized high-torque cable-whip rotary machines calibrated to pulverize hardened glaze without damaging structural flue masonry.
  • Flue Relining: If the glaze cannot be safely removed or if previous chimney fires cracked the underlying clay flue tiles, professional chimney repair involving relining the flue with a certified stainless steel sleeve is required.

Standards and Prevention Recommended by Fire Safety Experts

According to fire protection literature from the National Fire Protection Association, regular evaluations are critical to preventing the silent buildup of hazardous creosote glazes. Most homeowners cannot see beyond the throat damper, making internal camera inspections the gold standard for detecting early-stage glaze accumulation.

How to Prevent Creosote from Advancing

Maintaining a safe chimney involves smart combustion habits:

  1. Burn Only Well-Seasoned Wood: Test your firewood with a moisture meter to ensure moisture levels remain below 20%.
  2. Maintain Ample Airflow: Keep the damper wide open during burning and avoid restricting draft air until the fire has completely burned down to coals.
  3. Avoid Smoldering Burns: Build smaller, hotter fires rather than large, sluggish, smoking logs.
  4. Schedule Annual Checkups: Do not let seasons pass without having a technician evaluate your system. Schedule an inspection before starting your first autumn fire.

Why Does My Fireplace Smoke Come Into the House? 7 Common Causes

Lighting a fire on a chilly evening should fill your living room with warmth, relaxation, and the comforting crackle of burning logs. But when smoke rolls out of the hearth opening instead of floating up the chimney, it quickly creates coughing, stinging eyes, and lingering soot stains on walls and mantels. Here are the seven most common reasons your fireplace smokes into the house and how to fix them.

1. A Closed or Partially Open Damper

It sounds simple, but a closed or partially stuck damper is the single most frequent cause of fireplace smoke rollouts. The damper is a metal plate located in the throat or top of the chimney designed to seal off drafts when the fireplace is not in use.

If the lever or chain mechanism is stiff, rusted, or dislodged from its track, the damper may only open halfway. Always look up into the firebox with a flashlight to visually verify that the damper plate is completely vertical and open before lighting kindling.

2. A Cold Flue Dampering the Updraft

Chimneys work on basic physics: hot air rises because it is less dense than cool air. When your chimney flue is packed with dense, stagnant, cold air on a freezing night, that cold column acts like an invisible plug sitting above your firebox.

If you strike a match under cold air, the smoke has nowhere to rise and spills out into your warm room. To remedy this, "prime the flue" before lighting your fire: roll a single sheet of newspaper into a loose cone torch, hold it under the open damper, and let the flame heat the column for 30 to 60 seconds until you see the flame tip drawn upward into the flue.

3. Negative Pressure and Competing Exhaust Fans

Modern homes in Texas are built with tight weatherstripping, spray foam insulation, and energy-efficient windows. While great for lowering electric bills, a tightly sealed home can create negative indoor air pressure.

When powerful appliances like kitchen range hoods, bathroom exhaust fans, or clothes dryers run simultaneously, they pump air out of the house. To replace that air, your home will naturally pull air down the largest open vent available—your chimney flue. Cracking a nearby window one or two inches while lighting your fire equalizes pressure and restores an upward draft.

4. Wet or Unseasoned Firewood

Burning unseasoned or damp wood requires excessive energy just to boil off internal water before the wood can combust. This lowers the temperature of the fire significantly, resulting in thick, smoldering, heavy smoke that lacks sufficient buoyant heat to rise up the chimney.

The EPA Burn Wise Program recommends burning only split hardwood seasoned for at least six to twelve months with moisture levels under 20%. Dry wood ignites promptly, burns clean, and generates strong thermal updrafts.

5. Flue Blockages and Animal Nests

If your chimney cap is rusted or missing, foreign debris can easily obstruct the flue passage. Birds, squirrels, raccoons, and wasps frequently build nests inside chimneys during spring and summer. Additionally, windblown tree branches and leaves can collect on the smoke shelf.

A restricted flue cannot exhaust full combustion volumes. Arranging for certified chimney cleaning in Fort Worth eliminates physical obstructions and ensures clear airflow throughout the flue column.

6. Heavy Soot and Creosote Accumulation

Over months and years of use, soot and tar-like creosote line the flue walls, steadily decreasing the internal diameter of the chimney pipe. When the effective flue area shrinks, it can no longer vent the volume of gases produced by modern fireplace fires.

A professional sweep restores full flue clearance, optimizing draft and eliminating the risk of internal chimney fires.

7. Design Flaws, Broken Liners, and Inadequate Chimney Height

Sometimes the issue is structural. For a chimney to draft reliably, it must satisfy the standard 3-2-10 building code rule: extending at least three feet above the highest point where it penetrates the roof, and two feet higher than any building portion within ten horizontal feet.

A chimney that is too short, or a firebox opening that is oversized compared to the flue liner diameter, will consistently smoke into the room. Chimney Crown vs. Chimney Cap: What’s the Difference?

When homeowners hear terms like chimney cap, crown, chase cover, and chase top, it is easy to assume they all refer to the same thing. However, chimney crowns and chimney caps are two entirely separate components that perform distinct, complementary roles in defending your home against water leaks and weather destruction.

What Is a Chimney Crown?

The chimney crown is a flat or gently sloped concrete slab constructed on top of the uppermost course of chimney brick or stone masonry. Its primary role is to serve as a sturdy roof over the masonry column, sealing the gaps between the exterior bricks and the vertical flue liner tiles.

A properly constructed masonry chimney crown features a distinct downward slope that sheds rainwater away from the flue opening. It should ideally overhang the exterior brick edges by at least two inches, complete with a drip edge groove that prevents cascading rainwater from running down the exterior masonry facade.

What Is a Chimney Cap?

A chimney cap—also referred to as a spark arrestor or rain cap—is a metal protective hood mounted directly over the top of the open flue liner. Typically fabricated from stainless steel, copper, or galvanized steel, the cap consists of a solid metal lid positioned above open sides enclosed by wire mesh screening.

The chimney cap performs three vital defensive jobs:

  • Rain Prevention: It stops torrential rainfall and hail from dropping straight down into the flue pipe and fireplace firebox.
  • Wildlife Exclusion: The wire mesh keeps squirrels, birds, bats, and raccoons from entering your flue and building nests.
  • Spark Arresting: The metal mesh stops airborne hot embers and burning cinders from drifting onto shingle roofs or dry grass lawns.

Why Both Are Critical to Preventing Water Leaks

Water is universally acknowledged as the greatest single enemy of residential masonry chimneys. When either the crown or the cap fails, moisture gains unobstructed entry to your home.

If you have a chimney cap but a cracked crown, rainwater soaks into the porous mortar and bricks below. When temperatures plummet during North Texas winter freezes, trapped water expands, breaking mortar bonds, cracking brick faces (spalling), and causing internal water stains across living room ceilings.

Conversely, if your crown is pristine but you lack a cap, rainwater pours straight down the open flue pipe. This results in rusted metal dampers, ruined fireplace firebrick, foul musty smells, and toxic mold growth in humid summer months.

Recognizing Signs of Crown and Cap Damage

Because these components sit high on your roofline, damage frequently goes unnoticed until major leaks develop inside your home. Look for these warning indicators:

  1. Water pooling in the firebox after heavy Texas downpours.
  2. Rust staining on the chimney exterior or a damper that is frozen in place with corrosion.
  3. Flakes of terracotta clay or brick chips collecting on your fireplace floor.
  4. Cracks, chunks of missing concrete, or visible plant growth on the chimney top.

According to maintenance guidelines published by the Chimney Safety Institute of America, inspecting crowns and caps should be a non-negotiable part of your annual heating maintenance.

Crown Restoration vs. Full Rebuilding

If damage is discovered early, hairline fractures on a chimney crown can be sealed with a flexible elastomeric crown sealant coating, creating a waterproof membrane that withstands thermal expansion. However, if a crown is crumbling or composed of inferior builder's mortar, a full concrete crown rebuild is the only lasting solution. Best Firewood to Burn in Texas: Seasoning, Heat Output, and Creosote

There is nothing quite like loading up the hearth with local Texas timber when a sudden winter blue norther sweeps through North Texas. However, not all firewood burns equally. Choosing the right species and ensuring proper firewood seasoning makes the difference between an aromatic, cozy fire and a smoky, creosote-laden disaster.

Hardwoods vs. Softwoods: The Core Difference

In the firewood world, trees are categorized into hardwoods (deciduous broadleaf trees) and softwoods (conifers like pine and cedar). For indoor residential fireplaces, hardwoods are vastly superior.

Hardwoods possess dense cellular structures that burn slowly, yield prolonged coal beds, and produce high heat output measured in BTUs (British Thermal Units). Softwoods, by contrast, contain volatile resins, saps, and pitch. They burn quickly with intense popping sparks, leaving behind low-density coals and depositing copious amounts of sticky creosote inside your chimney flue.

Top Firewood Species for Texas Fireplaces

1. Texas Post Oak (The Gold Standard)

Abundant throughout North Texas and the Cross Timbers region, Texas post oak is widely regarded as the ultimate fireplace wood. It produces an impressive heat rating (around 24 to 28 million BTUs per cord), ignites reliably once seasoned, and burns with steady, clean flames and minimal popping.

2. Pecan and Hickory

Belonging to the same botanical family, pecan and hickory are dense, heavy hardwoods that deliver exceptional heat value and an iconic sweet, savory aroma. They produce long-lasting glowing embers ideal for chilly Texas nights, making them favorite choices for both hearth heating and backyard barbecue smoking.

3. Mesquite

Mesquite is famously hot-burning and abundant in Texas. However, because it burns with extraordinary intensity, it is best mixed in moderation with oak rather than burned exclusively in large fireplace loads, as excessive heat can thermal-shock older clay tile flue liners.

4. Ash and Hackberry

Both ash and hackberry are common in regional riparian zones. Ash is remarkable because it possesses naturally lower green moisture content and splits cleanly, providing moderate heat output and very low smoke emissions.

Wood Species to Avoid in Your Fireplace

To protect your indoor air quality and chimney structure, never burn the following materials:

  • Pine and Cedar: Softwoods full of combustible pitch that spark violently and accelerate dangerous Stage 3 creosote buildup.
  • Green or Freshly Cut Timber: Wood that hasn't cured expends all its energy boiling internal sap, filling your home with bitter, heavy smoke.
  • Treated Lumber & Pallet Scraps: Construction wood often contains chemical preservatives like arsenic or toxic adhesives that release lethal fumes when combusted.
  • Driftwood: Saturated with dried salts that produce chlorine gas when burned, rapidly corroding metal chimney flues.

The Art of Firewood Seasoning

According to forestry guides from the Texas A&M Forest Service, properly seasoned firewood should contain less than 20% internal moisture. Achieving this level requires splitting green wood and letting it cure for six to twelve months in a well-ventilated, sunny area.

You can identify seasoned firewood by its lighter weight, radial end checking (deep cracks on log ends), hollow sound when two logs are clapped together, and grayish, weathered bark.

Pair Quality Firewood with Regular Maintenance

Even with the cleanest-burning oak, routine combustion naturally deposits soot and residue over time. Pairing dry hardwoods with annual routine chimney sweeping and an autumn fireplace safety inspection ensures your system remains safe and efficient.

How to Tell If Your Chimney Is Leaking: Warning Signs and Fixes

When torrential rain pours down across Tarrant County, your home's roof and chimney work overtime to keep moisture outside where it belongs. Unfortunately, chimneys are vulnerable penetration points. Because a chimney penetrates multiple layers of roofing, attic space, and ceiling drywall, even a small leak can cause thousands of dollars in hidden water damage before dripping onto your floor.

Early Warning Signs of a Chimney Leak

Water rarely travels in a straight line, making leaks tricky to locate. Look for these subtle telltale signs that moisture has penetrated your chimney system:

  • Discoloration on Ceilings and Drywall: Brown, yellow, or tea-colored water rings appearing on the ceiling or drywall adjacent to the fireplace or along upstairs walls directly behind the chimney column.
  • Rusted Damper or Firebox Components: Metal throat dampers and firebox iron grates should not rust. If opening the damper requires muscle due to corrosion, water is falling into the chimney flue.
  • Pungent, Musty Hearth Odors: Rainwater mixing with soot deposits on the smoke shelf creates a distinctive, acrid odor reminiscent of wet charcoal that intensifies during humid summer afternoons.
  • Cracked or Crumbling Interior Firebrick: Refractory brick and mortar are engineered to resist high heat, but moisture degrades their chemical bonds, leading to spalling, pitted surfaces, and soft mortar.
  • Exterior Efflorescence: White, crystalline powder spreading across exterior chimney bricks indicates that water has saturated the masonry and is evaporating outward, leaching mineral salts to the surface.

The 4 Most Common Sources of Chimney Leaks

1. Damaged or Failing Roof Flashing

According to technical guidelines from the National Roofing Contractors Association, chimney flashing is one of the most critical waterproofing intersections on a roof. Flashing consists of L-shaped metal sheets woven into shingles and tucked into brick mortar joints (counter-flashing). Over time, expanding caulk seals crack, or shingles pull away, allowing wind-driven rain to run straight down into the attic.

2. Cracked Chimney Crown

The mortar crown at the top of the masonry chimney expands and contracts under harsh Texas sun and sudden freezes. When cracks form, water seeps into the core of the chimney structure, eroding mortar joints from the inside out.

3. Missing or Defective Chimney Cap

An open chimney top is essentially an open hole on your roof. Without a properly fitted rain cap, heavy rain falls directly down the flue liner, rusting metal components and pooling in the fireplace firebox.

4. Porous Bricks and Eroded Mortar Joints

Standard clay bricks are essentially hard sponges. After decades of rain exposure, unsealed masonry absorbs significant water volume. During freezing winter nights, that trapped water freezes and expands, cracking brick faces and washing away mortar.

Professional Solutions to Stop Chimney Leaks

Pouring hardware store silicone caulk over chimney joints is a temporary band-aid that often makes leaks worse by trapping moisture inside. Lasting solutions require proven masonry techniques:

  1. Flashing Replacement & Counter-Flashing Regletting: Installing new sheet metal and properly embedding counter-flashing into masonry mortar lines.
  2. Elastomeric Crown Coatings: Applying flexible, fiber-reinforced waterproof sealants that bridge cracks while flexing with thermal shifts.
  3. Stainless Steel Cap Installation: Mounting heavy-gauge rain caps that cover all flue pipes and spark arrestor screens.
  4. Vapor-Permeable Siloxane Water Repellent: Spraying specialized breathable masonry sealers that repel liquid rain while allowing internal moisture vapor to escape.

What Happens During a Professional Chimney Inspection?

Most homeowners know they should schedule an inspection before lighting their first winter fire, but few understand what actually occurs during a professional visit. Is the technician simply peering up the chimney with a flashlight, or is there a systematic engineering process at work? Here is an inside look at how professional chimney inspections work and what our technicians evaluate.

Standardized Inspection Levels Explained

Professional chimney sweeps adhere to safety standards codified by NFPA 211 and the Chimney Safety Institute of America. These guidelines define three distinct inspection tiers based on your home's circumstances:

Level 1 Inspection: The Annual Baseline

A Level 1 inspection is recommended for continuous, uninterrupted fireplace use where no changes or problems have occurred. If you haven't altered your heating system, experienced a storm, or noticed unusual smoke or leaks, a Level 1 inspection is the standard routine checkup.

During a Level 1 visit, our certified technician examines all readily accessible portions of the chimney interior and exterior, including:

  • The firebox, lintel, and hearth extension
  • The damper operation, hinge mechanics, and throat sealing
  • Accessible portions of the chimney flue liner and smoke chamber
  • The exterior chimney cap, crown, and visible roofline masonry

The goal is to verify that the flue is free of obstructions, that creosote buildup has not reached combustible levels, and that basic structural integrity is intact.

Level 2 Inspection: Comprehensive Video Camera Scans

A Level 2 inspection is more exhaustive and is required whenever there is a change in the heating system (such as installing a new gas insert or relining a flue), after an operational event (such as a chimney fire, earthquake, or major hailstorm), or upon the transfer or sale of a real estate property.

A Level 2 evaluation includes everything in Level 1 plus:

  • Accessing attics, basements, and crawlspaces to evaluate structural clearances between chimney masonry and combustible wood framing.
  • Deploying specialized high-definition, 360-degree rotary closed-circuit video inspection cameras down the entire length of the flue column.
  • Verifying the continuity of every individual clay tile liner joint, looking for hairline fractures, gaps in refractory mortar, or missing tiles that could let extreme heat or carbon monoxide escape into walls.

Level 3 Inspection: Destructive Investigation

A Level 3 inspection is rare and reserved for situations where concealed hazards are suspected that cannot be confirmed without removing parts of the building structure (such as cutting through drywall, removing chimney crowns, or stripping chase siding).

Step-by-Step Breakdown of an Inspection Visit

When our team arrives at your home for a chimney inspection, here is our standard workflow:

  1. Property Protection: We begin by laying clean canvas drop cloths over flooring, rugs, and the hearth to ensure your home remains immaculate.
  2. Hearth and Firebox Evaluation: We inspect firebrick for spalling, check the condition of refractory mortar joints, and verify proper clearance to combustible mantelpieces.
  3. Damper & Smoke Chamber Inspection: We verify the damper opens and closes securely and inspect the smoke chamber for smooth parging or heat damage.
  4. Flue Examination: Using professional lighting or video cameras, we inspect the entire length of the flue liner, identifying soot accumulation and checking for combustible creosote stages.
  5. Rooftop Analysis: We inspect the chimney cap, crown slope, brick tuckpointing, and roof flashing seal around the chimney base.
  6. Detailed Report and Photographic Evidence: We walk you through a digital summary documenting our findings and providing plain-English advice.

Why Combining Inspection with Cleaning Matters

An inspection often identifies that a chimney requires chimney cleaning to remove accumulated soot or creosote, or identifies subtle structural damage that can be corrected with minor chimney repair before turning into an expensive emergency.

blogs.contentHtml:
Gas Fireplace vs. Wood-Burning Fireplace: Maintenance and Care Compared

When homeowners evaluate fireplace options, the debate between gas logs and traditional wood-burning hearths often centers around ambiance versus convenience. While a real wood fire offers crackling logs and an authentic smoky aroma, a gas fireplace provides instantaneous heat at the flip of a wall switch. However, a widespread misconception persists that gas fireplaces require zero maintenance. Here is how maintenance compares between the two systems.

Wood-Burning Fireplace Maintenance: The High-Demand Hearth

A wood-burning fireplace is an active combustion system that demands routine hands-on care:

  • Creosote Management: Burning solid timber produces soot and volatile tar vapors that condense into combustible creosote. Regular chimney sweeping is essential to prevent chimney fires.
  • Ash Cleanup: After every few fires, accumulated ash must be shoveled out safely using a metal ash bucket once coals are completely cold.
  • Spark Arrestor & Cap Care: Open wood flames produce flying embers and cinders, requiring spark arrestors to prevent roof ignitions.
  • Firewood Sourcing & Storage: Homeowners must stack, cover, and season firewood for six to twelve months to maintain low moisture levels.

Gas Fireplace Maintenance: Low Effort, But High Precision

Gas fireplaces (whether vented gas logs, ventless sets, or direct-vent sealed units) do not produce creosote or flying ash, leading many homeowners to neglect them entirely. However, gas systems involve combustible fossil fuel, high-voltage ignition systems, and sensitive safety sensors that require dedicated calibration:

  • Pilot & Burner Orifice Cleaning: Dust, pet hair, and spiderwebs frequently clog pilot assemblies and burner ports. Clogged ports lead to improper fuel-air mixing, resulting in sooty yellow flames and carbon monoxide spikes.
  • Thermocouple & Thermopile Diagnostics: These safety sensors detect the pilot flame to keep gas valves open. When sensors coat with carbon or corrode, fireplaces refuse to ignite or shut down intermittently.
  • Glass Enclosure & Gasket Sealing: Direct-vent gas fireplaces feature sealed glass panels that must maintain an airtight gasket seal to prevent combustion exhaust gases from entering living areas. Over time, chemical film accumulates on the glass and requires special non-ammonia fireplace glass cleaners.
  • Venting Flue Clearance: Even though gas produces no creosote, the exterior venting pipe must remain completely unobstructed by bird nests, leaves, or rust scale to exhaust deadly carbon monoxide safely outside.

Comparison at a Glance

To help you weigh the ongoing demands of each hearth system, consider these operational factors:

  • Cleaning Frequency: Wood fireplaces require cleaning after every 1 to 2 cords of wood or annually. Gas units require annual servicing of burners, pilot valves, and ceramic ember beds.
  • Safety Risks: Wood systems present creosote fire and runaway ember risks. Gas systems present gas line leaks, pilot outages, and carbon monoxide risks.
  • Operational Cost: Wood requires purchasing or cutting cords of seasoned timber. Gas requires ongoing natural gas or propane utility supply.

Annual Inspections Apply to Both Systems

According to fire codes established by the National Fire Protection Association, all fuel-burning appliances, fireplaces, and chimneys should be inspected annually by a certified technician. Whether your home relies on crackling post oak or cozy blue gas flames, routine safety evaluations ensure safe venting and reliable heating.

How to Prepare Your Fireplace for Winter in North Texas

When summer's triple-digit heat finally subsides and crisp autumn air arrives in North Texas, thoughts turn to cozy evenings gathered around the hearth. However, after months of sitting idle during warm spring and summer weather, lighting your first fire without proper preparation can result in smoke-filled rooms, foul odors, or serious fire hazards. Here is your step-by-step winter fireplace preparation checklist.

1. Inspect the Rooftop Cap and Exterior Masonry

Preparation begins on the roof before lighting a single match. During spring and summer, strong Texas storms, hail, and high winds can shift chimney caps, blow off storm collars, or crack mortar crowns.

  • Verify that your chimney cap is securely fastened and that its wire mesh spark arrestor screen is clear of leaves and debris.
  • Check for animal nesting activity; birds and squirrels frequently construct nests atop chimneys during spring.
  • Examine the exterior masonry for cracked mortar joints, loose bricks, or rust stains that indicate water entry points.

2. Clean Out the Hearth and Firebox

Remove any leftover ash from the previous season. An ash bed deeper than one inch retains moisture, accelerating rust on metal grates and degrading firebox mortar. Shovel old ash into a designated metal container and vacuum the hearth with a designated ash or HEPA vacuum.

Inspect the firebrick and mortar lining the firebox walls. If you spot missing mortar or hairline cracks wider than 1/8th inch, professional masonry repair with refractory cement is necessary before starting fires.

3. Test and Lubricate the Damper Mechanism

Open and close the damper lever multiple times. The damper plate should pivot smoothly, swinging fully open without sticking and sealing tightly against the frame when closed. If the plate feels gritty or resists movement, use a high-temperature silicone lubricant to restore smooth movement.

4. Test Fireplace Draft and Prime the Flue

Before building a full fire, perform a quick draft test. Hold a lit match or candle near the open damper opening. If the smoke or flame pulls strongly upward into the flue, you have a natural updraft.

If the flame flickers into the room, your flue is filled with a dense column of cold air. To prime the flue, roll a sheet of newspaper into a torch, light the top, and hold it near the open damper for 30 to 60 seconds. The heat will displace the cold air plug and establish a robust upward draft.

5. Check Safety Alarms and Fire Extinguishers

Fireplace safety extends into your living room. The Chimney Safety Institute of America emphasizes that every home with a fireplace should feature functioning smoke detectors and carbon monoxide (CO) alarms on every level, particularly outside bedrooms. Replace alarm batteries each fall and verify that a working Class ABC fire extinguisher is readily accessible near the hearth.

6. Stock Well-Seasoned Firewood

Never burn unseasoned green wood, pressure-treated lumber, or painted wood scraps in your fireplace. Source dry hardwoods like Texas post oak, pecan, or ash that have been split and seasoned for at least six to nine months with moisture levels under 20%.

7. Schedule Your Annual Professional Checkup

While homeowner visual checks are essential, they do not replace a trained professional with specialized video diagnostic equipment. Scheduling a professional chimney cleaning and chimney inspection before cold snaps arrive ensures that hidden creosote deposits and internal liner fractures are resolved safely.

Animal Removal and Prevention for Chimneys in Tarrant County

You are sitting quietly in your living room when suddenly you hear a frantic fluttering, scratching, or chattering sound echoing from behind your fireplace damper. Wildlife intrusion is one of the most common and distressing chimney problems faced by homeowners in Tarrant County and surrounding communities.

Why Do Animals Enter Chimneys?

To wildlife, an uncapped chimney looks remarkably like a natural hollow tree trunk. It provides shelter from predators, protection from rain, and an ideal dark environment for nesting. In North Texas, the most frequent visitors include:

  • Chimney Swifts: Migratory birds that fly north from South America each spring. Swifts are federally protected birds that use specialized saliva to glue twig nests directly to vertical masonry flue tiles.
  • Raccoons: Female raccoons frequently climb chimneys in early spring to give birth and nurse newborn kits on the smoke shelf.
  • Squirrels: Squirrels often venture into flues searching for nesting sites or accidentally fall in and find themselves unable to climb up slick flue walls.
  • Bats and Birds: Small songbirds, owls, and bats can easily drop down open chimney flues during storms.

Dangers of Animals in Your Flue

Having wildlife inside your chimney poses serious health and safety hazards:

  1. Fire and Smoke Blockage: Twigs, leaves, feathers, and fur dry out and become highly flammable kindling. If you attempt to light a fire to "smoke out" an animal, the nest can catch fire, causing a devastating flue fire and filling your home with toxic smoke.
  2. Decomposition and Odors: Animals frequently become trapped and perish inside the flue. The resulting odor of decomposition is overpowering and attracts flies, fleas, and maggots into your home.
  3. Disease and Parasites: Wildlife can introduce mites, fleas, ticks, rabies, and histoplasmosis fungal spores into your living space.

How to Handle Chimney Wildlife Safely

According to wildlife care recommendations from The Humane Society of the United States, never light a fire to drive animals out. Doing so is inhumane, highly dangerous, and illegal in the case of protected species like chimney swifts.

If you suspect an animal is trapped, close your fireplace glass doors and damper tightly to prevent the creature from escaping into your living room, and call a professional chimney sweep or humane wildlife removal technician.

Permanent Prevention: Chimney Caps and Spark Arrestors

The only reliable, permanent solution to prevent animal intrusion is professional chimney cap installation. A properly engineered chimney cap combines a solid metal rain hood with heavy-gauge stainless steel wire mesh side screens.

The mesh screening allows smoke and exhaust gases to vent without restriction while creating an impassable physical barrier against birds, squirrels, and raccoons.

Once animals and nests are safely removed, scheduling a thorough chimney sweep and flue sanitization is essential. Our team removes leftover nesting materials, eliminates droppings, and sanitizes the smoke shelf and firebox with antimicrobial treatments.
